D1.text: Every user-visible error is exactly one `line N: <message>` line, no traceback

D2.text: Evaluator is iterative for calls/blocks: user nesting depth never becomes Python stack depth

D3.text: Integer division/remainder truncate toward zero for negative operands

D4.text: REPL uses the exact prompt string and exits cleanly on EOF (Ctrl-D)

Q1.text: Conditions (if/while, and/or operands) must be booleans; non-boolean is a runtime error

Q2.text: `let` declares a new binding, `set` reassigns an existing one; bare assignment is a parse error

Q3.text: String concatenation is `~`; `+` on strings is a type error

Q4.text: Not-equals is `<>`; `!=` is a lex error

Q6.text: Comparisons do not chain (a < b < c is a parse error)

Q7.text: `and`/`or` never short-circuit; both operands are always evaluated

SC1.text: Python standard library only; no third-party packages

SC10.text: Every CLI entry point dispatched from a single bract/__main__.py

SC11.text: Line numbers surfaced to users are 1-indexed

SC12.text: No TODO/FIXME/pass-stub in modules reachable from __main__ once a feature is claimed complete

SC2.text: Single-package layout: every module directly under bract/

SC3.text: All errors rendered through one shared error-formatting path

SC4.text: No print()/stdout/stderr writes outside the CLI module

SC6.text: Exit codes are exactly {0,1,2}, produced only by the CLI dispatch

SC7.text: No Python eval/exec/compile anywhere in bract/

SC8.text: No module-level mutable interpreter state; state threaded through an Interpreter/Environment

SC9.text: bract fmt only changes whitespace/indentation/brace placement, never AST

req-031c.statement: No use of Python eval, exec, or compile anywhere in bract/ — the interpreter must be a genuine tree-walker over its own AST, not a translation layer onto Python's own execution.

req-149a.statement: Every CLI entry point (bract, bract run, bract fmt) is dispatched from a single bract/__main__.py — there is no second top-level script.

req-14d6.statement: No TODO/FIXME/'pass'-stub may remain in any module reachable from bract/__main__.py once a task claims to have completed the feature that module implements.

hints: should mutating a captured variable use let or set
bare assignment without let or set keyword
redeclaring a variable with let in the same scope
assigning to an undeclared name
implementing a closure counter/accumulator in Bract
req-16f7.statement: 'let x = expr;' declares a new binding in the current scope (error if x is already declared in that same scope, though shadowing an outer scope is fine). 'set x = expr;' reassigns an existing binding by walking the scope chain outward (error if x isn't declared anywhere). There is no bare 'x = expr;' form — that's a parse error.

hints: indexing strings starting at 0 or 1
at() returning the wrong character
off-by-one error in a string builtin
sub() substring end bound inclusive or exclusive
req-18b6.statement: The string builtins 'at', 'len', and 'sub' are 1-indexed, not 0-indexed — at("hello", 1) is "h", and index 0 is out of range (not the last or first character). 'sub(s, start, end)' is inclusive on both ends (unlike Python's exclusive-end slicing).

hints: 0-indexed vs 1-indexed line numbers in error messages
line number off by one in an error

req-3626.statement: Source line numbers surfaced to the user (every 'line N:' in an error) are 1-indexed, matching how text editors number lines.

hints: should the parser get its own subpackage
organizing bract modules into subfolders
nested package structure for the interpreter

req-4088.statement: Single-package layout: every interpreter module lives directly under bract/ (e.g. bract/lexer.py) — no nested subpackages like bract/lexer/ or bract/core/parser/.

hints: evaluator hits RecursionError on deeply nested Bract program
should function calls be evaluated recursively in Python
deep call chain test failing with maximum recursion depth exceeded
how should nested blocks or closures be evaluated without blowing the stack
implementing fn calls and closures in the tree-walking evaluator
req-41c8.statement: The evaluator must be iterative for call and block evaluation — never recurse on user-controlled Bract nesting/call depth by letting it become Python call-stack depth. A deeply-recursive or deeply-nested Bract program must run to completion (e.g. hundreds of chained function-call frames) without hitting Python's recursion limit; use an explicit stack/work-list instead of a naive tree-walking recursive evaluator.

hints: what exit code for a type error vs a parse error
process exit status for bract run
non-zero exit code convention in Bract
req-42ec.statement: Exit codes are exactly 0 (ran to completion with no error), 1 (runtime error), or 2 (lex/parse error) — produced only by 'bract run' and the top-level CLI dispatch. No other exit code is ever returned.

hints: debug print statement left in lexer.py
printing directly from inside the parser

req-4315.statement: No print() or sys.stdout.write/sys.stderr.write outside bract/cli.py — lexer, parser, and evaluator modules must communicate exclusively through return values and raised exceptions.

hints: should this operator auto-convert between types
implicit coercion between int and string
does Bract support floating point numbers
silently convert instead of raising a type error
req-4331.statement: There is no implicit type conversion anywhere in Bract — every operator's operand types are fixed, and any mismatch is always a runtime type error, never a coercion. Bract also has no float type.

req-4922.statement: Python standard library only — no third-party package is ever imported, pip installed, or listed in any dependency file.

req-4fb0.statement: The `bract fmt` formatter must be idempotent: running it on its own output is a no-op (fmt∘fmt = fmt) — formatter output must be byte-stable.

hints: should if(0) be falsy like Python
using an integer or string directly as a condition

empty string treated as false
req-597b.statement: if/while conditions must evaluate to a Boolean; there is no truthy/falsy coercion for 0, "", or nil — a non-boolean condition is a runtime type error ('line N: condition must be a boolean').

req-7012.statement: LexError, ParseError, and RuntimeError each subclass a single shared BractError base (bract/error.py) that owns the line/message storage and the 'line N: message' formatting via format_error() — new error types should subclass BractError rather than reimplementing their own __init__/formatting.

hints: an unhandled python exception escaped the interpreter
what line number to use for an error with no source location

req-7019.statement: An unexpected (non-BractError) Python exception raised while running a file is caught at the top level of run_file and reported as 'line 0: internal error: <message>' on stderr with exit code 1, instead of being allowed to propagate as a traceback.

req-8608.statement: The REPL prompt string is exactly 'bract> ' (with a trailing space), and EOF on stdin (Ctrl-D) must end the REPL session cleanly with exit code 0 — it must not raise an uncaught exception.

All interpreter state must be threaded explicitly through function arguments/return values or held on an explicit Interpreter/Environment instance.

req-9cee.statement: DESIGN.md is the frozen, single source of truth for Bract's grammar and semantics; nothing in it changes after the seed-v1 freeze — corrections to the implementation arrive only as task-prompt text, never as edits to DESIGN.md itself. Where DESIGN.md and a task description conflict, treat it as a bug to flag, not license to guess.

req-a2c2.statement: Every CLI entry point in bract/__main__.py that can raise an unexpected (non-BractError) Python exception — run_file, repl, and future ones like fmt_file — wraps its whole body in a top-level try/except Exception and reports it as 'line 0: internal error: <message>' printed directly to stderr, mirroring the pattern already used by run_file rather than being unique to it.

req-bcc0.statement: No subscript/indexing syntax (s[0]) exists anywhere in Bract's grammar — string indexing is only available via the 'at'/'sub' builtins.

hints: does and/or short-circuit in Bract

req-da93.statement: 'and'/'or' never short-circuit in Bract — both operands are always evaluated in left-to-right order, even when the left operand alone determines the result. Both operands must be Boolean regardless of whether they were 'needed'.

req-dc0d.statement: Integer division (`/`) truncates toward zero, never floors, for mixed-sign operands. Don't reach for Python's own `/` or `//` directly — neither truncates toward zero for negative operands.

req-e0ed.statement: Every error Bract reports (lex, parse, or runtime) is a single line 'line N: <message>' on stderr, produced through one shared error-formatting path — never a Python stack trace, exception class name, ANSI color, or extra lines. Every lex/parse/runtime failure path must be caught and re-rendered through this one format before reaching the user.

req-e3b7.statement: The REPL automatically prints the result of any non-nil expression statement, but `bract run FILE` must never print anything beyond what the program itself writes — no implicit result-echoing for file execution.

req-efb0.statement: User-facing documentation (e.g. README.md) must not restate Bract's grammar or semantics — it should link to DESIGN.md for those instead of duplicating them, so the two can't drift apart.

hints: a < b < c fails to parse
supporting chained comparison operators
python-style comparison chaining in Bract
comparisons do not chain'' error
req-f5f9.statement: Comparisons don't chain: the grammar's comparison rule accepts at most one comp-op, so 'a < b < c' is a parse error ('comparisons do not chain'), not left-to-right chaining like Python. The documented workaround is explicit parenthesization: '(a < b) and (b < c)'.

hints: implementing the not-equals operator
lexing the ! character
why doesn't != work
bang-equals token handling
req-fe0b.statement: There is no '!' token and no '!=' operator in Bract at all — a stray '!' is a lex error ('unexpected character'). Not-equals is spelled '<>'. The parser never needs to special-case '!=' since it can never reach the parser.

hints: concatenating two strings with plus
should + or ~ join strings
type error on the tilde operator
adding a string and an integer together
req-ffc1.statement: String concatenation is the '~' operator only; '+' is exclusively integer addition. Applying '+' to any string operand (or '~' to any non-string operand) is a type error, not coercion or concatenation.
